title: Speech Understanding tasks explained: Speaker ID, custom formatting, and translation
summary: How speaker identification, custom formatting and translation, batch or real time, turn raw transcripts into structured data.
body_markdown:
The real cost of transcription often isn't the API call. It's the time your team spends manually processing the output.


You get back a transcript, but it's labeled "Speaker A" and "Speaker B." Phone numbers are spelled out. Dates appear in inconsistent formats. If you're serving global customers, you need translations on top of transcriptions. Each of these gaps requires manual post-processing or custom code before the transcript becomes usable data.


Speech Understanding tasks solve this by transforming raw transcripts into structured, actionable intelligence automatically. Rather than treating transcription as an isolated step that produces generic text, Speech Understanding applies specialized processing during transcription to deliver outputs that match your specific business needs. This article covers three critical tasks: advanced speaker identification, custom formatting, and translation, both on recorded files and in real time.


## The gap between transcription and usable data


Traditional speech-to-text gives you words on a page, but most applications need more than that.


Consider a healthcare platform processing patient consultations. A basic transcript might show "Speaker A said this, Speaker B said that." But the system needs to know which speaker is the dietitian and which is the patient, not just for human review, but for automated chart updates and compliance tracking. Doing that labeling by hand adds to a clinician's documentation time.


Or take a call center handling thousands of daily interactions. Raw transcripts need to be ingested into CRM systems that expect specific data formats. When email addresses transcribe as "john at company dot com" instead of "john@company.com," automated workflows break. Teams spend hours reformatting transcripts before they can be processed.


Global companies face an additional challenge: serving customers across multiple languages without building separate transcription pipelines for each market. The traditional approach—transcribe in the source language, then translate—adds latency, cost, and complexity.


Speech Understanding tasks address these gaps by building intelligence directly into the transcription process.

## Advanced speaker identification


Basic[speaker diarization](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/pre-recorded-audio/label-speakers) tells you when speakers change. Advanced speaker identification tells you who's speaking.


The distinction matters for three reasons: compliance, automation, and analytics.


**Compliance requirements** in industries like healthcare and finance mandate knowing exactly who said what. A call center needs to verify that the authorized account holder, not just "Speaker A"—provided consent. Legal intake systems need to attribute statements to specific parties for case documentation.


**Automation breaks** when systems can't distinguish speakers by role. Healthcare platforms that auto-update patient charts need to know which statements came from the clinician versus the patient. Contact centers building agent performance scorecards need accurate agent identification, not generic speaker labels.


**Analytics lose value** when aggregated across anonymous speakers. Without knowing who each speaker represents, you can't identify coaching opportunities, track sentiment by role, or analyze conversation dynamics.


Advanced speaker identification solves this through two approaches: role-based labeling and name-based labeling.


**Role-based labeling** automatically tags speakers by their function: agent versus customer, doctor versus patient, interviewer versus candidate. It builds on speaker diarization: once the audio is split by speaker,[Speaker Identification](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/speech-understanding/speaker-identification) reads the conversation for context clues to decide each speaker's role, with no voice enrollment or training data for specific individuals.


**Name-based labeling** goes further by identifying speakers by name when you provide a list of expected participants. The names need to come up in the conversation for the model to match them. This is valuable for internal meetings, recorded consultations with pre-scheduled participants, or any scenario where you know who should be speaking.


Because it works on top of diarization, label quality depends on the audio: clear, distinguishable voices and enough speech from each speaker. To improve accuracy further, add a short description of what each speaker typically discusses.


## Custom formatting


The difference between a transcript and usable data is formatting.


Contact centers processing tens of thousands of hours monthly need transcripts that flow directly into CRM systems. When phone numbers, email addresses, and dates don't match expected formats, automated workflows fail. What should be a 30-second transcription becomes a 5-minute data entry task.


[Custom formatting](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/speech-understanding/custom-formatting) eliminates this friction by applying your formatting rules during transcription. You define the rules once; every transcript follows them consistently.


**Date standardization** handles regional variations automatically. A US-based company might need "10/22/2025" while European operations expect "22/10/2025." Global organizations can specify ISO format "2025-10-22" for database compatibility. Without custom formatting, teams must manually convert dates or build parsing logic to handle inconsistent outputs.


**Phone number patterns** ensure transcripts match your CRM's expected format. Whether you need "(555) 123-4567," "555-123-4567," or international formats, custom formatting applies the pattern automatically. This prevents integration failures when systems expect specific phone number structures.


**Contact information** converts spelled-out emails and URLs into properly formatted, clickable text. "john at company dot com" becomes "john@company.com." "company dot com slash products" becomes "company.com/products." This seemingly small improvement eliminates a major friction point in automated processing.


**Currency and number precision** gives you control over decimal places and formatting for financial transcripts. Loan applications, insurance claims, and financial consultations need consistent number formatting for downstream processing.


**Multi-rule application** lets you apply multiple formatting standards simultaneously. A single transcript can follow US date formatting, international phone patterns, and ISO currency codes, whatever combination matches your systems.


The real pain point here isn't the formatting itself, but the inconsistency. When transcripts arrive in unpredictable formats, you're forced to either build complex parsing logic or accept manual cleanup. Custom formatting makes every transcript predictable.


## Translation


Serving global customers shouldn't require separate transcription pipelines for each language.


The traditional approach, transcribing audio in the source language, then sending the transcript to a translation API, works but introduces unnecessary complexity. You're managing two separate API calls, handling potential failures at each step, and accepting additional latency from sequential processing.


Organizations expanding into new markets face this complexity at scale. Healthcare platforms operating across multiple countries need consultation transcripts in local languages. Media monitoring companies analyzing African market advertisements need both transcription and translation for millions of audio files. International recruiting platforms need interview transcripts in various languages, without building country-specific infrastructure.


Speech Understanding handles this through integrated[translation](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/speech-understanding/translation) that runs in the same request as transcription. Turn on language detection, list your target languages, and the response returns a` translated_texts` entry for each target alongside the original-language transcript—all in a single API call. Translation works with AssemblyAI-STT-3.7 and Universal-2.


**86 target languages** are supported, covering the major global markets and many regional languages. This includes European languages, Asian languages with different character systems, and languages with limited commercial speech recognition support. The[translation feature page](https://www.assemblyai.com/features/translation) and the docs' supported languages table have the current list.


**Automatic language detection** removes the need to pre-specify the source language for each audio file. This is valuable when processing mixed-language datasets or handling customer interactions where the spoken language isn't known in advance.


**Formal register and per-utterance output** are configurable. Set` formal` for formal phrasing, and set` match_original_utterance` (with speaker labels on) to get a translation for each utterance, so translated text stays attached to the right speaker.


**Single API integration** simplifies your architecture by eliminating the transcription-to-translation pipeline. Fewer API calls mean fewer potential failure points, reduced latency, and simpler error handling.


The business impact's straightforward: you can expand into new markets without rebuilding your speech processing infrastructure. A single integration supports global operations.


## Real-time translation


Batch translation works on finished recordings. Live captions, multilingual support calls, and voice agents need the translation while the person is still talking. For that, AssemblyAI's streaming API translates speech in real time on the same WebSocket that returns the transcript.


It runs on[AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/introducing-assemblyai-stt-3-7) (` assemblyai-stt-3-7-realtime` ) and[LLM Gateway](https://www.assemblyai.com/products/llm-gateway) , configured with a single` llm_gateway` connection parameter. Here's what happens during a session:


1. You open one streaming connection and pass` llm_gateway` with a model, a translation prompt, and an optional` max_tokens` cap.
2. AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime streams` Turn` messages in the spoken language, exactly as it would without translation. Partial turns stay untranslated.
3. When a turn ends, the server sends the final transcript to LLM Gateway with your prompt. It returns the translation on the same WebSocket as an` LLMGatewayResponse` message.
4. Each` LLMGatewayResponse` carries the` turn_order` of the turn it translates. The translation is produced in the background, so it doesn't delay the final` Turn` . Translations for short consecutive turns can arrive out of order, so match them to turns by` turn_order` .


There's no second API to call. If a gateway call fails or times out, no` LLMGatewayResponse` is sent for that turn. Per the[real-time translation docs](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/streaming/real-time-translation) , a small model such as` qwen3.5-4b-32k-fast` typically lands the translation within about 100 ms of the final turn. If you omit the model, it defaults to` gemini-2.5-flash-lite` . Translation requests go to LLM Gateway with zero data retention.


The source language can be any of the 32 languages AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime transcribes, including speakers who[switch languages mid-sentence](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/streaming/multilingual-transcription) . You set the target language in the prompt. Here's a minimal Python example over the raw WebSocket that translates English speech into Spanish:


```text
# pip install websocket-client
import json
from urllib.parse import urlencode


import websocket


YOUR_API_KEY = "<YOUR_API_KEY>"


LLM_GATEWAY_CONFIG = {
"model": "qwen3.5-4b-32k-fast",
"prompt": "Translate the following English into natural Spanish and reply with only the translation: {{turn}}",
}


CONNECTION_PARAMS = {
"sample_rate": 16000,
"speech_model": "assemblyai-stt-3-7-realtime",
"llm_gateway": json.dumps(LLM_GATEWAY_CONFIG),
}


API_ENDPOINT = f"wss://streaming.assemblyai.com/v3/ws?{urlencode(CONNECTION_PARAMS)}"


def on_message(ws, message):
data = json.loads(message)


if data["type"] == "Turn" and data["end_of_turn"]:
print(f"[{data['turn_order']}] {data['transcript']}")


elif data["type"] == "LLMGatewayResponse":
translation = data["data"]["choices"][0]["message"]["content"].strip()
print(f"[{data['turn_order']}] -> {translation}")


ws_app = websocket.WebSocketApp(
API_ENDPOINT,
header={"Authorization": YOUR_API_KEY},
on_message=on_message,
)


# Stream 16 kHz, 16-bit mono PCM audio to the socket as binary frames.
# See the full microphone example in the LLM Gateway streaming guide.
ws_app.run_forever()
```


` {{turn}}` is a template variable the server fills in with the final transcript of each turn, so leave it exactly as written. To translate into another language, change "Spanish" in the prompt. For conversations, the docs recommend adding recent context with` {{history_3}}` , which inserts the last three final transcripts that have already been translated, since history is the main lever for translation quality. The[LLM Gateway streaming guide](https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/streaming/guides/real_time_llm_gateway) has the complete microphone example, and the Python and JavaScript SDKs expose the same setting.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)


### What are Speech Understanding tasks?


Speech Understanding tasks are processing steps that run with transcription and return structured output instead of plain text. AssemblyAI's include speaker identification (names or roles instead of "Speaker A"), custom formatting (consistent dates, phone numbers, and emails), and translation. You turn them on with a` speech_understanding` parameter in the same request that creates the transcript.


### What's the difference between speaker diarization and speaker identification?


Speaker diarization detects when the speaker changes and labels each one generically, such as Speaker A and Speaker B. Speaker identification builds on diarization and replaces those labels with the names or roles you provide, like "Agent" and "Customer." It infers who is who from the conversation, so it needs speaker labels turned on and enough speech from each person.


### How many languages can AssemblyAI translate into?


Batch translation supports 86 target languages, and you can request several in one call. The supported languages table in the translation docs has the current list. For real-time translation, the source can be any of the 32 languages AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime transcribes, and you set the target language in the translation prompt.


### Can AssemblyAI translate speech in real time?


Yes. Pass the` llm_gateway` connection parameter with a translation prompt when you open an AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime stream. After each final turn, the server sends the translation on the same WebSocket as an` LLMGatewayResponse` message tagged with that turn's` turn_order` . Partial turns stay in the spoken language. See our[real-time speech translation](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/real-time-speech-translation) guide for a full build.


### How is real-time translation priced?


Real-time translation has no separate add-on price. You pay for the AssemblyAI-STT-3.7-Realtime session at $0.30/hr, billed on how long the WebSocket is open, plus the LLM Gateway input and output tokens used for each turn's translation. Batch translation is a $0.06/hr add-on to pre-recorded transcription. LLM Gateway usage isn't covered by the free credits.


### Does custom formatting work with any transcript format?


Custom formatting can run in the same request as transcription or on text you already have, in a separate request. It standardizes dates (US, European, or ISO), phone number patterns, emails, URLs, and currency precision. You can apply several rules to one transcript at the same time.
